transkript.t: In this town, nobody is ever allowed to turn around.
You see, the lurker is always standing right behind somebody.
He's nine feet tall and skinny as a broom, with arms so long his fingers drag on the ground,
and a long gray face with a grin that never goes away.
He picks one person, and he follows them, one step behind, everywhere.
Everyone else in town can see him, except you.
And the second you turn around and look at him, you're gone.
So nobody here turns around, ever.
Every house has a back door, so you never have to walk back the way you came.
If you forget something, you walk backwards to get it, and yelling,
Hey! Look behind you! We'll get you thrown in jail.
Old Mrs. Patterson had the lurker behind her for 40 years.
She never turned around once.
When she finally died of old age, he just walked away, looking for someone new.
My dad always told me two things.
If he ever picks you, buddy, don't you dare turn around,
and never walk backwards near Dead Man's Drop.
Dead Man's Drop is the old quarry at the edge of town.
It goes down so far, you can't see the bottom.
Then, one night at dinner, my mom dropped her plate.
My dad went very still, and my little sister started crying.
They were all staring at the same spot, right behind my chair.
My dad whispered, Don't turn around.
That's when I felt it, something cold breathing on the back of my neck.
The lurker had picked me.
At first, I tried to live normal, but at school, nobody would sit behind me.
At night, I could hear him breathing next to my bed,
and kids would yell, Spider on your back!
Just to watch me freeze.
One morning, I heard my mom's voice call me from the hallway behind me.
I almost turned.
Then I remembered, my mom was at work.
The lurker just breathed a little harder.
Every second of every day, I had to remember.
Don't turn around.
Mrs. Patterson did it for 40 years.
I lasted one week.
Then I remembered what my dad said.
Never walk backwards near Dead Man's Drop.
And I realized something.
The lurker always stays exactly one step behind me.
If I step forward, he steps forward.
If I step backwards, he steps backwards.
So that night, I put on my dad's old hoodie
and walked to the edge of town, to Dead Man's Drop.
I stood one step from the edge, facing away from it,
which meant the lurker was standing right on the edge behind me,
with nothing behind him.
Then, I took one step backwards.
His long, cold fingers grabbed my shoulders.
He knew.
He held on and pulled me back with him, over the edge.
My heels slipped.
Rocks fell into the dark below.
We were both hanging there, his fingers digging into my dad's hoodie.
So I unzipped it.
I lifted my arms and I slipped right out.
I fell forward onto the dirt.
And behind me, I heard him fall down and down and down.
Still holding my dad's hoodie.
I lay there for a long time.
I still didn't turn around.
Then I heard footsteps.
My dad running across the field.
He dropped to his knees and hugged me.
Buddy, there's nothing behind you.
So, for the first time in a week, I turned around.
There was nothing there, just the drop.
The next morning, the whole town stood in the middle of Main Street.
And for the first time in 100 years, everyone turned around.
